slides: Now let's look at polygons that meet at one point. On the exam, two regular polygons often sit on a common side. These questions have two steps, and they come back every time.

slides.say: Here's a regular hexagon, and a square built on one of its sides, outside the hexagon. Look at the corner they share. Three angles sit around it. The hexagon's angle, the square's angle, and the gap between them, x.
at: Look at the corner they share

slides.say: All the angles around one point add up to three hundred sixty. The hexagon's angle is one hundred twenty. The square's angle is ninety. So x is three hundred sixty, minus one hundred twenty, minus ninety. That's one hundred fifty.
at: The hexagon's angle is one hundred twenty
So x is three hundred sixty

slides.say: The exam usually goes one step further. Let's close the gap into a triangle, with a line across it.
at: The exam usually goes one step further

slides.say: The two sides of angle x are a side of the square and a side of the hexagon. Both are equal to the common side, because each polygon is regular. So the two sides are equal, and the triangle is isosceles.
at: The two sides of angle x

slides.say: Its top angle is one hundred fifty. The two base angles share one hundred eighty minus one hundred fifty, thirty. So each base angle is half of thirty, fifteen. Careful, thirty is both base angles together. Don't forget to divide by two.
at: one hundred eighty minus one hundred fifty

slides.say: Let's see it again with a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon on a common side. Around the shared corner, three hundred sixty minus one hundred twenty is two hundred forty. Minus one hundred eight is one hundred thirty-two.
at: a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon

slides.say: Again, the two sides of the gap are equal to the common side, so the triangle is isosceles. One hundred eighty minus one hundred thirty-two is forty-eight. Half of that is twenty-four. So each base angle is twenty-four.
at: the two sides of the gap

slides.say: And when regular polygons fill the space around a point with no gaps, their angles add up to exactly three hundred sixty. Three regular hexagons fit, because three times one hundred twenty is three hundred sixty. That's how a honeycomb is built.
at: their angles add up to exactly

slides.say: Four squares fit too, four times ninety. And six equilateral triangles, six times sixty. But three regular pentagons don't fit. Three times one hundred eight is three hundred twenty-four, so a gap of thirty-six is left.

slides: So when two regular polygons share a side, first use the three hundred sixty around the point. Then look for the isosceles triangle. Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
